Heritage sites in Punjab: Amritsar, Harappan Ropar and Sikh history

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

Punjab's heritage runs from the Harappan settlement at Ropar and the Kushan-period stupa site at Sanghol to the forts of the Sikh chiefs and the gurdwaras of Amritsar and Anandpur Sahib. Key places include Harmandir Sahib, Jallianwala Bagh, Gobindgarh Fort, Qila Mubarak in Patiala, Bathinda's Qila Mubarak and the Mughal serai at Doraha. Punjab has no UNESCO site.

We build Punjab study tours that join Amritsar, Ropar and Sanghol with Chandigarh, with a briefing lecture for your group.

Punjab's layers of history

The Indian state of Punjab is only the eastern part of the historic Punjab, the land of five rivers that was divided in 1947. Even so, it holds evidence from almost every period. Harappan and later settlements line the Sutlej, Buddhist and Kushan remains appear at Sanghol, the Grand Trunk Road brought Mughal serais and bridges, and from the 16th century the region became the heartland of Sikh history.

Punjab has no UNESCO World Heritage Site, although Chandigarh's Capitol Complex, a UNESCO site, is in the shared capital next door. Our indus valley civilization explainer gives the background for the earliest sites.

Museums in Punjab

  • ASI Site Museum, Ropar. Finds from the Harappan and later levels at Ropar.
  • Sanghol Museum. Kushan sculpture and finds from the stupa site.
  • Partition Museum, Amritsar. Oral histories and objects from 1947, in the Town Hall.
  • Virasat-e-Khalsa, Anandpur Sahib. Galleries on Sikh history.

Ropar and Sanghol: Punjab's archaeology

Ropar (Rupnagar), on the Sutlej, was one of the first Harappan sites excavated in independent India, in the 1950s. It showed a sequence from Harappan levels to medieval times, and a burial with a dog alongside a human attracted wide interest. The ASI site museum at Ropar displays finds from these excavations.

Sanghol, in Fatehgarh Sahib district, has a Buddhist stupa and monastery and produced a large hoard of Kushan-period sculpted railing pillars in red sandstone, carved in the Mathura style with women, trees and auspicious motifs. Both sites suit groups who want to see how a mound becomes a sequence. Our session Chronology and archaeological dating explains how that sequence is built, and the Harappan world tour from Delhi adds Rakhigarhi next door in Haryana.

Amritsar: gurdwara, garden and fort

Amritsar grew around the tank and temple founded by the Sikh Gurus in the late 16th century. Harmandir Sahib, its upper storeys covered in gilded copper under Maharaja Ranjit Singh, faces the Akal Takht across the causeway. The old city's katras (merchant quarters) and bazaars grew around it.

Jallianwala Bagh, a short walk away, is the walled garden where troops under General Dyer fired on an unarmed crowd on 13 April 1919. Gobindgarh Fort, rebuilt by Ranjit Singh, is on the city's edge. See our Amritsar heritage walk guide for a route through the old city.

Forts, palaces and serais

Patiala's Qila Mubarak is the core of the princely state's capital, with the Qila Androon palace, painted walls and a durbar hall. Bathinda has its own Qila Mubarak, a massive brick fort whose origins are early medieval and which is linked in tradition to Razia Sultan's imprisonment. Kapurthala's Jagatjit Palace, modelled on French palaces, shows the taste of a late princely ruler.

Along the old road, the Mughal serai at Doraha and the Shambhu and Nurmahal serais recall the imperial highway, and Nurmahal's gate is a fine piece of Mughal brick and stone carving. Our programme Forts of Rajasthan is a good companion for anyone studying how forts were planned.

Sikh heritage beyond Amritsar

Anandpur Sahib, with Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib, is linked to the founding of the Khalsa in 1699. Talwandi Sabo has Takht Sri Damdama Sahib. Fatehgarh Sahib and Chamkaur Sahib are tied to the events of 1704 to 1705. Sultanpur Lodhi is associated with Guru Nanak's early life, and the Virasat-e-Khalsa museum at Anandpur Sahib tells Sikh history through galleries.

Questions people ask

Are there any UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Punjab?

No. The state of Punjab has no UNESCO World Heritage Site. The nearest is Le Corbusier's Capitol Complex in Chandigarh, the shared capital, which is part of a transnational serial listing inscribed in 2016.

What are the main archaeological sites in Punjab?

Ropar (Rupnagar), a Harappan and later settlement on the Sutlej with a site museum, and Sanghol, a Buddhist stupa site that produced Kushan-period carved railing pillars. Both are protected by the Archaeological Survey of India.

What happened at Jallianwala Bagh?

On 13 April 1919, troops under General Reginald Dyer fired on an unarmed crowd gathered in the walled garden in Amritsar, killing hundreds. The massacre became a turning point in the national movement. The garden is now a memorial.

Which forts can you visit in Punjab?

Gobindgarh Fort in Amritsar, Qila Mubarak in Patiala, Qila Mubarak in Bathinda and the remains at Phillaur are the main ones. Check visiting arrangements before you go, as some are managed by different agencies.
